narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in your third year of law school was the single biggest reason for the negative outcome. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) in Year 3, compared with an average around the middle of the class among accepted students, strongly signaled future difficulty passing the bar. Your first-year performance was the second most influential factor; ranking in the second decile against an average of sixth decile among accepted students also pushed the prediction toward failure. Finally, your LSAT score of 28, well below the average of 37 among those who were admitted, added further weight in the same direction.

All three of these academic indicators worked against you and pulled the model’s prediction heavily toward bar exam failure. No other features, including your family income, gender, or race, played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT after targeted preparation. Raising these key performance markers would significantly increase your probability of passing the bar and open future admission opportunities. (218 words)
